author: John Henson
title: Improving quality of water in Evarts discussed during meeting - NewsBreak
text:
By John Henson ,
4 hours ago By Braelynn Smith
Harlan Enterprise
City officials and community advocates in Evarts gathered Tuesday for a follow up to January’s Water Resilience Forum, providing residents with a deep dive into water quality testing, aging infrastructure and the future of the regional “water story.”
The meeting at the Evarts Public Library was led by Michelle Carroll-Cole and Madison Mooney of LIKEN Knowledge with the goal to bridge the gap between utility operations and public perception. Attendees discussed the unique challenges of maintaining water quality in the Appalachian region and how community engagement is vital for long term success. Mooney highlighted her work in relationships within her home county of Martin to preserve oral history and land accessibility alongside water issues. The forum serves as a critical step toward a new chapter for the Evarts water initiative and the broader region.
A primary focus of the evening was the transparency of water testing procedures and the specific chemicals monitored by the city. Woody Fields, the Evarts Water Plant Manager, addressed lots of questions that were gathered from people around the community in hopes to ensure resident concerns were heard. He emphasized that while the list of potential contaminants is vast, the city utilizes Pace Analytical, a certified independent lab in Pineville, for its sampling.
“There’s hundreds of different things we test for every year,” Fields said during his presentation to the forum. He also noted that he keeps records dating back to 1996 and is happy to share them to ease any public anxiety about safety. This commitment to data accessibility is designed to build trust between the utility providers and the families they serve.
The discussion turned to the health aspects of water treatment, specifically the use of chlorine to ensure potability. Addressing the common complaint of a chlorine smell, Fields defended the use of the chemical as a vital safeguard against dangerous pathogens. He noted that he personally drinks the water several times a day and feels much safer knowing the treatment is working effectively. The “chlorine scent” is often a result of the “delicate dance” required to ensure water remains safe by the time it reaches the furthest ends of the system near the Virginia line. For residents sensitive to the taste, officials recommended inexpensive faucet or pitcher filters as a practical and immediate solution. They noted that Pure Plus models performed exceptionally well in recent pilot testing conducted by the Liken Knowledge team.
While parts of the Evarts downtown system date back to 1977, officials highlighted significant progress in modernization and efficiency. The city has successfully reduced water loss from a staggering 75 percent down to roughly 21 percent over the last three years. This improvement was made possible by the dedicated work of the field superintendent and his team who are constantly hunting for leaks. Mike Maggard outlined upcoming capital projects funded by grants, including a new water tank currently being fabricated in Illinois. Other planned improvements include total water line and asphalt replacement on McCoy Street and the installation of advanced leak detectors. These technological upgrades will allow the city to identify problems instantly rather than searching for “a needle in a haystack.”
The forum concluded with a plea for residents to enroll in the city’s “All-Call” system for real time alerts on water advisories or outages. Officials stressed that the system is only effective if residents take the personal responsibility to keep their contact information current.
“You cannot get a call if you don’t have the same phone number,” warned Mooney during the closing remarks.
The system is free to customers and can even target specific streets to avoid waking up the entire town for a localized issue. Residents are encouraged to call city hall to verify their enrollment or update their data whenever they change service providers. Maintaining this line of communication is essential for public safety and community transparency during the ongoing water journey, according to city officials.
